title: The Streets: 7 Days
premise: Seven days in March. He is nineteen, the money at home is tight, and everybody who has ever helped him wants something this week.

design.deeIsNotAVillain: Dee never threatens and never punishes a refusal. "No, that's fair", and he means it, and he does not ask twice.
design.bagBoundary: The bag is an active object on Days 1-2 only. After Day 2 it is never the subject of a scene, choice, consequence or line of dialogue, and the sender is never identified.
design.authoringRule: The player is not choosing between right and wrong. He is choosing what he is willing to spend, and what he has left on Monday.

scoring.note: Scores are retained for schema compatibility and for the results log, and the values are real. playerVisible: false means they are never surfaced in player-facing scoring UI and never applied to the client's global stat pool. The Streets ends on trajectory and authored evidence, not on a number labelled INTEGRITY.

cast.name: Amara
cast.role: Has her own life and her own read

money.note: The only number the player sees. A plot fact, not a stat.

kaiStrain.note: Kai has no trust axis. He is friction, not a relationship being built.

s1d1_open.message:
Half five, and he has been up since eleven, which he is aware of.

Mum is doing the thing she does before a shift — moving through the flat picking things up and putting them somewhere else, coat already half on. There is a letter on the side that has been there four days, face down, which is its own kind of statement.

She is not angry. She is doing sums in her head while talking about something else, and he can tell, because he has watched her do it since he was twelve.

s1d1_kitchen.message:
"You're still putting something in Friday, yeah?"

She says it lightly and once, which is worse than if she pushed, and then waits.

It is Tuesday.

choices.label: "I haven't got it."
choices.beat: She stops moving. "How short?" — which is not the question he wanted.

s1d1_kitchen_react.message:
"Alright." She finds her keys where she left them, which takes a while.

Four minutes later the door goes and the flat is the flat again.

messageVariants.message:
"Alright then." She takes it. She takes it slightly too easily, and is out the door before he has worked out whether that means anything.

Four minutes later the flat is the flat again.

s1d1_walkway.message:
Jay is on the walkway and has been for a while, which he does when he wants to be found without having asked.

He is funny for about ninety seconds and then isn't, and the gap between those two things is visible if you know him. Jay's flat is where he ate for a stretch when things were bad, and neither of them has ever said a word about it.

Tunde's message arrives while Jay is talking. *Cage, eight. You coming or not.*

choices.label: Walk with him. Ask what's wrong.
"I'm going to the cage."
choices.beat: Jay says "yeah, safe" in the voice that means the opposite.

s1d1_jay_asked.message:
He's annoyed for about four seconds — the specific annoyance of someone who wanted to be asked and hasn't decided how to be — and then tells him.

His sister has a course place. There's a deposit. The date has already been moved once and can't be again.

He tells it in pieces, out of order, and stops before the part where he explains what he's going to do about it. The player notices him stop.

s1d1_jay_quiet.message:
They walk. It's a good two hours and genuinely funny in places.

Twice, unprompted, Jay says he's fine.

The second one is what stays with him on the way home, because nobody says it twice.

s1d1_cage.message:
Tunde is training for something specific and doesn't make a thing of it.

Afterwards he asks a direct question about what the player is actually doing with himself, and takes the answer seriously enough to be unsatisfied by it.

He isn't unkind. He just doesn't pretend.

s1d1_alone.message:
His room. The flat is empty because Mum is on nights.

It's the first hour he's had to himself in a week, and it's fine, and he checks his phone eleven times.

thread.narration: Two things on the phone.
Twenty minutes between them. He hasn't answered either.
And a number he doesn't have saved.

thread.text: can you hold something till morning

thread.narration: No greeting. No name. Nothing else.

choices.label: "yeah"
choices.beat: *10 mins.* Nothing else. He is outside for four minutes and back inside by ten past.

choices.label: "till the morning. then it's gone."
choices.beat: *yeah course.* Immediate, easy, and the ease is not reassuring.

thread.narration: That is the entire reply.

choices.label: "alright"
choices.beat: The question is still in the thread. It doesn't protect him from anything.

thread.text: you about today. need you for something. before 4 tho

thread.narration: Mum isn't in. Her shoes aren't by the door, which means she went straight from the night to the day and won't be back until after six. There's a mug in the sink she didn't have time to wash, and that's the whole of what the flat has to say this morning.
Two threads.

thread.text: you about today. need you for something. before 4 tho

thread.narration: And under last night's unanswered question of his own:
Mum isn't in. Her shoes aren't by the door.
Two threads.

thread.text: you about today. need you for something. before 4 tho

thread.narration: Mum isn't in. Her shoes aren't by the door, which means she went straight from the night to the day.

s1d2_bag.message:
Somebody is on the walkway who he half-recognises and can't place.

Two people on the balcony above are hanging washing.

choices.label: Take it down.
choices.beat: Eleven seconds. Nobody says thanks. Nobody explains. The walkway is the walkway again.

choices.label: "Come up then."
choices.beat: They come up. It takes longer. Somebody now knows which door.

s1d2_walkway.message:
Jay is outside before he's finished getting ready, which is how you know it matters.

What he needs is a lift with an errand. His aunt has put food aside and it has to be picked up before she shuts at four, and it's a bus and a walk each way, and he doesn't want to do it on his own.

That's genuinely all he says.

s1d2_run.message:
Two buses and forty minutes of not much. Jay is fine for about twenty of them.

Then it comes out — the sister, the course place, the deposit, the date that got moved once already and can't be moved again. He tells it in pieces, out of order.

This time he doesn't stop before the end.

s1d2_ask.message:
He doesn't ask. That's the whole difficulty.

He describes the situation and then goes quiet and lets the silence do the asking, and both of them know exactly what is happening.

There is forty pounds in the player's pocket. The deposit is not forty pounds.

choices.label: Give him what you've got.
choices.beat: He tries to refuse it once, badly, and then takes it. It doesn't cover it. Both of them know it doesn't cover it.

choices.label: "Let me ask Tunde."
choices.beat: Tunde says yes without hesitating, which is somehow worse.

choices.label: Message the number back.
choices.beat: **nothing right now.** That is the entire reply. Nothing happens today.

choices.label: Go with him. Don't pay.
choices.beat: "Nah, you're alright. I'll sort it." He means about half of it.

choices.label: "I can't do this today."
choices.beat: "Yeah, no, course." He is normal for the rest of the walk, and it's the normal that stings.

s1d2_plate.message:
On the landing outside his flat, Jay splits it — one container for his, one held out.

"That one's your mum's. She likes the rice."

He says it like it's nothing, because to him it is. His aunt made too much, the way she has made too much for eleven years.

s1d2_close.message:
He puts a container of somebody else's aunt's food in his own fridge, in a flat where the money is tight, on the day he decided what he was and wasn't going to do about Jay's sister.

Mum's shoes are still not by the door.

s1d3_open.message:
Two days since he decided what he was and wasn't going to do about Jay's sister.

Jay hasn't messaged. That's not a falling-out; it's just Thursday. But it's the first morning since Sunday that he's woken up without somebody wanting something, and the quiet is not as good as he expected it to be.

messageVariants.message:
Two days, and nothing in his pocket since Wednesday.

Jay hasn't messaged. That's not a falling-out; it's just Thursday. But it's the first morning since Sunday that he's woken up without somebody wanting something, and the quiet is not as good as he expected it to be.

Two days since he did something about it, and nothing since.

Jay hasn't messaged. Not a falling-out — just Thursday. It's the first morning since Sunday nobody has wanted anything, and the quiet is not as good as he expected.

s1d3_tunde.message:
Tunde finds him, which Tunde does, because Tunde plans things.

There's a trial. Saturday, ten till two, at the place he's been talking about since March. The man who runs it will be there and Tunde has already said his name — not put him forward formally, just said it, in the way that gets you looked at once.

"It's one Saturday. If you're coming, come properly."

He isn't selling it. He's about half embarrassed to have mentioned it, because he knows exactly how it sounds to say *there might be something in September* to somebody who needs money now.

s1d3_stop.message:
Two of them are already out of the car by the time he clocks them.

It isn't a shout. Nobody grabs anybody. Names, where he's going, where he's come from, and one of them looking past him at the road the whole time.

He is carrying nothing. There is nothing to find and nothing is looked for.

Across the walkway, outside the shops, Kai is with three or four others and his phone is up, and it has been up since about the second sentence.

Two years ago Kai did this to somebody else in front of everyone, and the player laughed. Not loudly. He laughed.

choices.label: Answer everything. Flat.
choices.beat: Four minutes. He hears himself being polite and doesn't enjoy it.

choices.label: "Can I ask what this is about?"
choices.beat: "Just a chat." Said with no edge at all, which is worse. Eight minutes instead of four.

choices.label: "Kai. Put the phone down."
choices.beat: The phone goes down. Kai says nothing at all, in front of four people.

s1d3_after.message:
They get back in the car and go. Four minutes, start to finish.

Nothing happened. Nothing is on any record anywhere. There is no charge, no note, no follow-up, and in a week nobody official will remember it at all.

messageVariants.message:
They get back in the car and go. Four minutes, start to finish.

Nothing happened. No charge, no note, no follow-up, and in a week nobody official will remember it at all.

By half one it is on three phones. By four it is on a lot more than three.

They get back in the car and go. Four minutes, start to finish.

Nothing happened, and nothing exists of it. Forty people saw him square up to Kai over nothing, and Kai has to live with having put it down.

s1d3_dee.message:
Dee comes to him, which is not how it normally goes.

He is not a stranger. Two summers ago Dee got him a fortnight's work when he needed it, paid him on the Friday like he said he would, and drove him home the night the buses stopped. Neither of them has mentioned it since and neither of them needs to.

He's got a unit for a fortnight — phone cases, chargers, the usual — and he needs somebody on it Saturday, ten till six. Eighty quid, cash, end of the day.

He asks for the player by name. He doesn't say why him, and it doesn't occur to him that he should, and eighty is a bit more than the day is worth.

Saturday is Saturday.

choices.label: "Yeah, I'll do it."
choices.beat: "Ten o'clock. Don't be late, I'll have to sack you." He's joking. It's also the only instruction.

choices.label: "What is it, actually?"
choices.beat: He answers completely and plainly — the unit, the stock, the hours, where the float lives — and says nothing at all about why him.

choices.label: "I can't Saturday."
choices.beat: "No, that's fair." He means it, and he doesn't ask what's on, and he doesn't ask twice.

thread.narration: Whatever he said, it's said.
He opens the thread with Amara in it.
Tuesday. There is nothing new underneath. She hasn't messaged since.
He types something and doesn't send it, which is a thing he has now done twice.

s1d4_open.message:
You can hear it from the stairs. Somebody has put the music slightly too loud and nobody has said anything about it because it's her night.

He has been coming to this door since he was nine. He ate in this kitchen for four months.

He is carrying a card because his mum told him to bring a card.

data.location: The landing outside Jay's flat, seven

s1d4_frontroom.message:
She has him by the arm inside six seconds and doesn't let go for another minute. He gets introduced to two aunties as *the sensible one*, which is a thing she has called him since before it was true. There is a plate in his hand he does not remember accepting.

Mum is here. She knows this family. She is in the corner with Jay's mum and one of the aunties, and she has taken her shoes off, which he has not seen her do since Christmas.

Through the doorway he can see the shape of the evening. Kai has the kitchen and four people. Tunde is by the balcony door with a drink he isn't drinking, out of place in the specific way of somebody who came because you asked him to, weeks ago, before any of this. Amara is in the hallway looking at the photographs, and hasn't messaged since Tuesday.

Jay is somewhere. Jay has been somewhere all evening.

s1d4_kitchen.message:
Kai is doing Thursday from memory to four people who half believe him, and that is worse for Kai and better for nobody.

He doesn't stop when the player comes in, which is either confidence or courtesy and there is no way to tell.

messageVariants.message:
Kai is doing Thursday. He plays it twice — once for the people who came in late — and the player is in the room while his own name is used.

He doesn't stop when the player comes in, which is either confidence or courtesy and there is no way to tell.
Kai stops talking when the player comes in. Everybody notices. Nobody says anything, and after about four seconds he starts again, on something else.

s1d4_balcony.message:
Tunde talks about tomorrow like it's settled, because as far as he knows it is.

It's cold and neither of them goes back in for eleven minutes.

messageVariants.message:
Tunde talks about tomorrow like it's settled, because as far as he knows it is. He mentions the time twice.

It's cold and neither of them goes back in for eleven minutes, and the player does not correct him.

Tunde talks about tomorrow and doesn't oversell it, which is how he is when he has stopped worrying about somebody.

It's cold and neither of them goes back in for eleven minutes.

s1d4_photos.message:
"You're in about four of these," Amara says.

She isn't making a point. She's working something out, and she says the thing about Tuesday exactly once and then lets it go.

Twenty minutes.

character.name: Amara
character.role: Has her own life and her own read

s1d4_stay.message:
He stays. He holds the plate. He is told about somebody's hip and somebody's daughter and he says the right things in the right places.

Through two doorways he can watch all of it happening without him.

His mum looks over twice and doesn't say anything either time.

s1d4_speech.message:
Somebody bangs a glass.

Jay does four sentences about his mum and gets through about three. Everybody claps. She cries in the way you're allowed to at your own birthday.

He looks over once, in the middle of it.

messageVariants.message:
Somebody bangs a glass.

Jay does four sentences about his mum and gets through about three. The part he can't finish is about people who turn up.

He looks over once, in the middle of it, and it is not subtle, and nobody else sees it.

s1d4_landing.message:
Jay comes out after him.

He isn't angry. He's his mum's son and it's her night and he's had four cans, and he is going to ask one question and then go back inside.

"Where'd you get to?"

choices.label: Tell him.
choices.beat: "Yeah, no, fair." Then, going back in: "You could've said."

choices.label: Give him a version.
choices.beat: He accepts it and holds the door open and neither of them moves for a second.

choices.label: "Nothing. I'm just tired."
choices.beat: "Alright." He goes back in.

s1d4_close.message:
Two floors and a walkway. Mum has her shoes in her hand.

She says one thing about Tuesday. Not the money — Tuesday.

And then she talks about somebody's hip for the rest of the walk, and he can't tell whether the first thing was the point or whether he just made it the point.

messageVariants.message:
Two floors and a walkway. Mum has her shoes in her hand.

"You said it was sorted, on Tuesday." She doesn't look at him. It isn't a question and she doesn't wait for an answer.

Then she talks about somebody's hip for the rest of the walk.

Two floors and a walkway. Mum has her shoes in her hand.

"They're good to you, that family." A pause. "They always were."

Then she talks about somebody's hip for the rest of the walk.

s1d5_open.message:
The thing he said on Thursday is now the thing he's doing.

Mum went in at six. There's a note about Sunday afternoon — she needs him around for something, she hasn't said what, and the note doesn't ask so much as assume.

s1d5_stall.message:
Eight hours and it is boring. Phone cases, chargers, a card reader that works about half the time. Four people ask if he's got a specific thing and he hasn't. Around two he serves somebody's mum who knows his mum. Around four he stops checking the time.

At six Dee comes by, counts out eighty in twenties, and says "same next Saturday if you want it" — which is the first time anybody has offered him something twice.

s1d5_trial.message:
Two hours, and about forty minutes of it is standing about. The man Tunde talked about watches for maybe nine minutes total.

Nobody says anything at the end except *cheers lads*, and Tunde is quiet on the way back in a way that could mean anything.

There is no money in it. There won't be any money in it until September, if there's any at all.

s1d5_tunde_missed.message:
Tunde isn't angry, and it takes about four seconds to work out that not being angry is worse.

He asks if everything's alright. He genuinely wants to know if everything's alright.

choices.label: Tell him where you were.
choices.beat: "Right." A pause. "You could've told me Thursday and I'd have said do the money." And he means that too.

choices.label: Give him a reason.
choices.beat: He takes it. He doesn't ask a follow-up, which he would have if he believed it.

choices.label: "Can it be moved?"
choices.beat: "I'll ask." He will ask. He'll be asking on the player's behalf for the second time in a fortnight.

s1d5_tunde_went.message:
Tunde rings straight after and gets to it.

The man asked what he's like. Tunde has to tell him something by Wednesday and he'd rather tell him the true thing.

choices.label: "Yeah. I'm serious."
choices.beat: "Alright. I'll tell him that then." And now somebody has said it on his behalf.

choices.label: "I don't know yet."
choices.beat: "Yeah, no, fair enough." He goes quiet a bit early.

choices.label: "I can't do September for nothing."
choices.beat: He hadn't thought about it, and you can hear him thinking about it. "Let me ask."

s1d5_dee.message:
He has a cousin. Thirteen. He's started being around people Dee doesn't want him around, and Dee can't say that to him — "because look at me."

Training's Tuesdays and Thursdays, six till half seven. Take him, bring him back, be about. He'll sort him weekly for it.

He isn't selling it. He looks slightly embarrassed to be asking, which is not a thing the player has seen on him before.

"You're the only one round here I'd have him with."

He means it. That is the entire difficulty.

choices.label: "Yeah, course."
choices.beat: "Safe." He doesn't make anything of it, which is how you know he was worried about asking.

choices.label: "Tuesdays. I can't do Thursdays."
choices.beat: "Tuesdays is better than nothing." Slight disappointment, immediately packed away. He respects it.

choices.label: "I can't take that on."
choices.beat: "No, that's fair." He asks after the player's mum on the way out. He does not ask again.

s1d5_close.message:
The flat is empty. The note about Sunday is still on the side.

Whatever he agreed to or didn't, Tuesday is in three days and it is somebody else's Tuesday now.

messageVariants.message:
The flat is empty. The note about Sunday is still on the side.

There is eighty quid in twenties in his jacket and nobody in the flat to mention it to.

s1d6_open.message:
Mum is in the kitchen and she has already made tea for two, which she does not do.

She needs him at three. Her sister's, an hour, back by five. She doesn't say why and it clearly isn't important, and she asks once, in the way that means she has decided not to ask twice.

It is the first thing she has asked him for all week.

thread.narration: Twenty past eleven.
Four minutes later, before he's replied:
He doesn't say what he wants. He has never once said what he wants.
Half twelve.
Five words, and it is not a check-up. It is a man who has told a thirteen-year-old that somebody is coming.
One o'clock. Tunde rings rather than messages. He needs to tell the man something and he'd rather tell him the true thing, and he has said this before, in almost these words.
None of them knows about any of the others. That is the whole of Sunday.
Twenty past eleven.
One o'clock. Tunde rings rather than messages. He needs to tell the man something by Wednesday.
And a number in a group he isn't really in:
Four minutes of Thursday, sent to somebody who sent it to somebody who sent it to him.
Dee doesn't call. None of them knows about any of the others.
Twenty past eleven.
Half twelve.
One o'clock. Tunde rings rather than messages.
And a number in a group he isn't really in:
Four minutes of Thursday. None of them knows about any of the others.
Twenty past eleven.
One o'clock. Tunde rings rather than messages. He needs to tell the man something by Wednesday and he'd rather tell him the true thing.
Dee doesn't call. None of them knows about any of the others.

s1d6_afternoon.message: He cannot do all of it. He can't even do two of it properly.

s1d6_fronted.message:
He goes to Jay's flat and says it to Jay's mum in her own kitchen — the deposit, the date, the fact that Jay has been carrying it alone since before the birthday.

Jay is standing right there while he does it.

It is the correct thing to do and Jay does not look at him once.

s1d6_sat.message:
Two hours on the wall outside the flats, and they don't solve anything.

At some point Jay says "I know you were working Saturday" — not as an accusation, just as a thing he knows — and after that it is easier rather than harder.

s1d6_covered.message:
He tells his mum he'll be back by four. He tells Jay he's coming. He tells Dee Tuesday's fine.

Then it's six and he has been in his room and every one of those three sentences is still technically true and none of them happened.

s1d6_mum.message:
An hour at her sister's. She talks to her sister and he sits there and is, for the first time in six days, somewhere he said he'd be.

His phone goes twice and he doesn't look at it, and she notices that he doesn't look at it.

s1d6_late.message:
Mum comes in and puts her bag down and doesn't take her coat off.

She has heard something. Not the whole thing — a version, from her sister, from somebody on the walkway, from the specific and unreliable network that has been running all week without him in it.

She asks him one question directly.

choices.label: Tell her all of it.
choices.beat: She sits down. She doesn't shout, and she doesn't say it's alright either.

choices.label: Tell her the part that's true now.
choices.beat: She asks one follow-up and accepts the answer, and you can see her decide to accept it.

choices.label: "I'm fine."
choices.beat: She takes her coat off and puts the kettle on and doesn't ask again.

s1d6_close.message:
Tuesday is in two days. Tomorrow is the deposit. Wednesday is Tunde's answer.

Nothing has been resolved. One thing has been said out loud that hadn't been.

messageVariants.message:
Somewhere in it she said "Tuesday you told me it was sorted", and she said it once.

Tuesday is in two days. Tomorrow is the deposit. Wednesday is Tunde's answer. Nothing has been resolved.

Tuesday is in two days. Tomorrow is the deposit — and somebody else is dealing with it now, because he made that happen in her kitchen with her son standing there.

Nothing has been resolved.

s1d7_open.message:
Nobody has messaged.

That is the first thing. Six days of somebody wanting something by four, and this morning the phone has one notification and it's the bank telling him what his balance is.

Mum went at six. The mug is washed.

s1d7_situation.message:
The deposit was today and it either happened or it didn't, and he will find out from somebody else rather than from Jay.

Tunde has to tell the man something on Wednesday.

Tuesday is tomorrow, and a thirteen-year-old either has somebody coming or he hasn't.

Amara's two messages from Tuesday are still the last thing in that thread.

None of these are problems he can solve today. They are things that have arrived at the shape they are going to be in.

s1d7_action.message:
He has one afternoon and he can do one thing with it.

Not fix the week. Do one thing.

terminal.consequence: She reads it and doesn't reply for two hours and then replies properly, and the reply is longer than his was.
terminal.landing: "You could've just said that on Tuesday." She isn't being unkind. She's stating the thing that was true all week.

choices.label: Give your mum what you've got.
choices.lockedLabel: Give your mum what you've got. — you haven't got it

terminal.consequence: Sixty of it on the side, under the kettle, where she'll find it and he won't have to hand it over. She doesn't mention it. It's gone in the morning and she doesn't mention that either.
terminal.landing: On Thursday she buys him something he didn't ask for and doesn't mention that. He counts what's left twice on the bus and it isn't very much.

choices.label: Go and see the man yourself.
choices.lockedLabel: Go and see the man yourself. — that door went a while ago

terminal.consequence: Without Tunde, without telling Tunde, on a Monday afternoon, at a place he has been to twice. The man is busy and gives him four minutes. Four minutes is more than he had this morning.
terminal.landing: Tunde rings that night. "He said you turned up." That's the whole call, and Tunde sounds like somebody who has just got something back.

choices.label: Tell Dee you can't do Tuesdays.
choices.lockedLabel: Tell Dee you can't do Tuesdays. — there's nothing to give back

terminal.consequence: The day before it starts. Face to face, because doing it by message would be the other thing. "Nah, that's better than Tuesday night." He means it, and he is also now sorting something out at short notice for a thirteen-year-old.
terminal.landing: He doesn't ask why. He asks after the player's mum, the way he always does, and then he's gone.

choices.label: Say it to Jay. Don't ask for anything.
choices.lockedLabel: Say it to Jay. — there's nothing owed that way

terminal.consequence: On the walkway, standing up, in under a minute, without asking whether they're alright now. Jay says "yeah, I know" and then nothing for a while, and then something about his sister that is not an answer to anything.
terminal.landing: They stand there another minute. Neither of them says the week is finished, because it isn't.

choices.label: Say it to Kai.
choices.lockedLabel: Say it to Kai. — there is nothing between you to settle

terminal.consequence: Two years late for one thing and five days late for another, and he doesn't separate them. Kai is thrown, and covers it badly, and says "yeah, you're alright" — which from Kai is a lot.
terminal.landing: It doesn't come up again. Six weeks later they're civil in a shop queue and it is genuinely fine, which nobody could have predicted in March.

choices.label: Get on a bus and go somewhere else.

terminal.consequence: Not running. Not sulking. One afternoon somewhere nobody knows him, and back by nine. Four hours where nobody wants anything. He doesn't do anything with them. He doesn't need to.
terminal.landing: Coming back over the bridge he works out that the whole thing turned on about nine seconds on Tuesday, and that he did not experience those nine seconds as a decision at the time.

reflections.title: The One Who Said It
reflections.text: He stood in somebody else's kitchen and said the thing his friend couldn't, in front of his friend, and it was the right call and it wasn't his to make. Both of those stayed true. Nobody in that flat has mentioned it since.

reflections.title: Three True Sentences
reflections.text: He told his mum he'd be back by four, told Jay he was coming, told Dee Tuesday was fine. Every one of those was true when he said it and none of them happened, and the week ended with three people each holding a slightly different version of a person who was, that Sunday, in his room.

reflections.title: Two Small Ones
reflections.text: A version on Friday night, on a landing, at a party. A Saturday morning somebody had arranged for him. Neither was a lie he'd have called a lie at the time, and by Sunday there were two people carrying something he'd told them that wasn't so.

reflections.title: Said What He Could Do
reflections.text:
He put a limit on something on the Tuesday, in writing, before he knew any of it mattered. On the Saturday he said no to a good thing he couldn't carry.

Neither of those is impressive. Both of them are rarer than they sound.

reflections.title: Tuesdays, Not Thursdays
reflections.text: He said what he could actually do rather than what he wanted to be the kind of person who does, and then he did it. There's no story in that, which is why almost nobody manages it.

reflections.title: Somebody Trusted Him With Somebody
reflections.text:
A man who knows exactly what he is asked him to be near a thirteen-year-old twice a week, and he said yes, and the money was real and so was the reason.

He's on somebody's payroll now. He knew that when he said it.

reflections.title: He Kept Turning Up
reflections.text: On the days it was available, he did the boring thing. That's most of it. It doesn't feel like a decision at the time, which is exactly why it's so easy not to.

reflections.title: He Stayed in the Front Room
reflections.text:
He was invited, he came, he held a plate for four hours and talked to two aunties about a hip, and through two doorways the rest of the week happened without him.

He owed that flat. It was also the easiest place in it to stand.

reflections.title: He Asked
reflections.text:
At midnight, to a number he didn't have saved, he typed *what is it* and sent it. He didn't get an answer.

The question's still in the phone. It didn't protect him from anything. It just means he was the only person in it who said a true thing at the start.

defaultReflection.title: Seven Days
defaultReflection.text: On the Tuesday, nobody could have told you a single thing about who he was. By the Monday, four or five people could, and they'd each say something different, and not one of them would be wrong.

jay.text:
Jay knows about Dee, because he told him on a wall on a Sunday when there was nothing else to do.

It doesn't become a thing. What it becomes is the reason that, in August, when Jay hears something about Dee from somebody who has it wrong, he comes and asks rather than assumes.

Jay's sister goes in September. Nobody in that flat has ever said out loud that it was because of a Sunday afternoon in March, and Jay has never once thanked him for it, and both of those are correct.

They're alright. It took until about July.
Jay is still Jay. He's careful with him now in a way he wasn't before — asks before assuming, which he never used to do — and neither of them has worked out whether that's better.

Jay stops coming to the door. Not dramatically, not with a conversation. He just stops, and after a while it's hard to remember which week it was that he stopped.

His mum still says hello on the walkway. She always will.
They're fine. That's the accurate word for it. Same walkway, same shop, same jokes — and one subject that neither of them is ever going to go near again.

mum.text:
She never mentions the money. Not that week, not later.

What changes is that she starts saying the numbers out loud — not asking him for anything, just saying them, the way you do with somebody who has turned out to be in it with you.

She knows about the Tuesday and she knows about the Sunday, and she has decided to keep exactly one of those.

She doesn't bring it up. She does start telling him things about the money before he asks, which she has never done, and it takes him about a month to work out that's what it is.

She is careful with him now, and being careful is not a thing she has ever had to be with him.

She still cooks for two. She just doesn't wait up any more, and she has stopped asking what time he'll be back, and neither of those was a decision she announced.
She stops managing what he knows. It's small and it's most of what he wanted — she says the number out loud one Thursday, in the kitchen, like it's nothing, and then carries on making tea.

Something loosened. She tells him things she used to handle on her own — not the whole of it, but more than none — and the first time she does it she watches his face to see whether it was a mistake.

It wasn't.

She works it out in her own time, the way she works everything out, and never tells him that she has.

What changes is that she stops waiting up. He notices in about May and doesn't mention it.

She's the same. Still on the extra shifts, still doing sums in her head while talking about something else.

She asks him less. He couldn't tell you when that started.

tunde.text: Tunde puts his name forward again in September, for something else, and doesn't mention that he did it the first time and it didn't take.
Tunde starts in September. There's a photo of him in the polo shirt in a group chat and it's genuinely good news and he looks at it for slightly too long.
Tunde stops asking. He isn't cold about it. He's just got a start date and a bus route and a life that begins on the ninth.
Tunde's around. They still play. He doesn't bring up the trial and he doesn't bring up September, and the not-bringing-it-up is new.

dee.text:
The cousin gets to training on Tuesdays and Thursdays and is, by Christmas, quite good. Dee pays on the Friday, every Friday, exactly like he said he would.

He's on Dee's phone now under his actual name. He hadn't thought about what that meant until he saw it.

Dee tells people he wouldn't do Thursdays. He tells it as a good story about somebody knowing what they can manage, and it is one — and it also means a lot of people who didn't know his name know it now.

Dee's warm to him for the rest of the year and never asks him for anything again.

He sees the cousin around sometimes, at the shops, with other people. He's got no way of knowing whether that means anything.

Dee's Dee. Says hello, asks after his mum, remembers things.

There's no second offer. It's not a snub — he's just somebody who got asked once.

amara.text:
Amara's still there in August. She asked him one straight question in March and got a straight answer, and it turns out that was the whole of it.

She's doing her thing. He knows what her thing is now, which he didn't in February.

kai.text:
It stays ended. Six weeks later they're civil in a shop queue and it's genuinely fine, which nobody could have predicted in March.

He's the first person to text when something good happens in September.

afterwards.text:
He doesn't tell anybody where he went that afternoon, and nobody asks.

It becomes a thing he does. Four or five times that year, always on his own, always back the same night. He would not be able to tell you what it's for.

finalMessage.text:
Nothing broke.

That's the achievement and it's the whole problem. Three or four people are walking around with a version of March that he gave them, and every one of those versions is going to have to survive contact with somebody else's. Not this month. Probably not this year.

The longer it holds, the more it'll cost to say.

It's not a story about a bag.

It's a story about nine seconds on a Tuesday, and about being the one nobody looked at right up until they did. He's got money coming in and a place to be on Saturdays and somebody's phone with his actual name in it.

None of that is a trap. All of it narrows what next year can look like, and he won't feel it narrowing.

People come to him now.

He earned that on a Wednesday with forty quid he didn't have and on a Sunday in somebody's kitchen, and it's real — there are three or four people who'd answer for him and mean it.

Which means every one of their problems is now slightly his. One day he's going to not pick up, and somebody is going to experience that as a betrayal, and they won't be entirely wrong.

He's good at this. That's the thing nobody expected, including him.

Money, access, people who'd vouch — all of it came from being the one who sorts things out, and it works, and he likes that it works.

What he hasn't noticed yet is that every one of those relationships is about what he does. At some point he'll have to ask for something back, and find out which of them were about him.

He didn't drop anybody.

Jay's still there and so is Tunde, and holding both of them cost more than either would have on its own — the week was longer for him than it was for anyone else in it and nobody knows that.

It isn't sustainable and it hasn't stopped. Both of them are going to keep asking, and neither of them has any idea they're asking somebody who is already at the limit.

There's a route now. September is real rather than a thing people say.

What it cost is small and permanent: he's around less, he says no more, and the block has noticed and adjusted. Nobody's angry. They've just stopped including him in the first round of asking.

He'll have to prove the new direction was worth it to people who aren't going to see any of it.

He said what he could do and what he couldn't, every time, out loud.

He was right nearly every time as well — you could go through the week day by day and find the sentence where he was right.

There's nobody left to say it to. The line between not needing help and not letting anyone give you any is somewhere behind him, and he's going to have to find it going backwards.

Nobody looks at him again.

That's what he had on the Monday before any of it, and it took a week of saying no to people — including the ones being kind — to get it back. It's worth exactly what it was worth to somebody at midnight on Tuesday.

He's the only one who knows it cost anything. If he leaves it much longer, it stops being a week he had and starts being who he is.

He didn't solve any of it.

What he did was say one true thing on a landing at half eleven when a version would have been easier, and put a limit on something at midnight before he knew it mattered. Nobody thanked him for either.

Some people are still disappointed and they're entitled to be. The next honest thing is going to be available on an ordinary day, not in a crisis, and that's the one that's hard.

defaultFinalMessage.text:
Seven days.

Nothing landed and nothing broke. He's got roughly what he had on the Monday, minus a bit of money and plus the specific knowledge of what he does when four people want the same afternoon.

None of it is finished. Tuesday is training, Wednesday is an answer somebody's waiting for, and the deposit was yesterday. It just carries on from here, which is what most weeks do.
